hook: Feelings come in degrees, yet the tools that generate emotional images have understood only labels like “happy” or “sad.”
lede: Ask a text-to-image model for “a boy is running in the forest” and it will draw one. Ask for the same boy in the same forest, a little less cheerful and a little more tense, and there is no precise way to say it: tools built for emotion work from tags, and struggle to control what the picture actually shows. We built EmotiCrafter so that emotion becomes a coordinate instead of a word. Alongside a free-text prompt, it takes two numbers, valence and arousal, and renders the scene to match.

chapters.title: Emotion as a coordinate, not a label
paragraphs: Psychologists have not agreed on a fixed set of emotion categories, and the pioneering system for emotional image generation, EmoGen, works from a single tag without a text prompt. That leaves two gaps: you cannot say what the picture should contain, and you cannot say how much of a feeling it should carry.

EmotiCrafter uses the Valence-Arousal model instead, a well-known psychological model that places emotions in a two-dimensional space. Valence runs from unpleasant to pleasant, arousal from calm to excited, each on a scale from −3 to 3. In that space a character can drift from “bored” to “tired”, the kind of subtle shift that discrete labels cannot express.

quote.text: The limited scope of discrete emotion tags falls short of capturing nuanced emotions.

figures.caption: The Valence-Arousal model. Excited and delighted sit at high arousal and positive valence; bored and tired sit low on both.

chapters.title: Emotion enters through the prompt
paragraphs: Instead of injecting emotion into the image generator itself, EmotiCrafter changes what Stable Diffusion XL reads. A prompt first becomes text features, the numerical form in which the generator takes in language. An emotion-embedding network, built on a modified GPT-2, predicts how those features should shift for the requested valence and arousal, and adds that shift to the original. The description stays in place; the emotion arrives as an offset.

Learning that shift requires the same scene described with and without feeling. GPT-4 wrote such pairs for 39,843 images from OASIS, EMOTIC and FindingEmo, each with valence and arousal annotated by people: a neutral prompt that describes the image objectively, and an emotional one that emphasizes the color, lighting and texture that shape how it feels. Every prompt went through crowd-sourced verification. For an image of a small dog, rated at valence 1.65 and arousal −0.12, the pair reads:
points: Neutral: “A small white dog walking down a path.”
Emotional: “A small white dog joyfully exploring a serene forest path, surrounded by lush greenery and dappled sunlight, evoking a peaceful and content atmosphere.”

figures.caption: Inside one of the 12 Emotion Injection Blocks: after self-attention, the valence feature and then the arousal feature are injected into the prompt’s hidden state through two successive cross-attention steps.

chapters.title: Two numbers can overrule the words
paragraphs: Because emotion is its own input, it can contradict the prompt and prevail. Given “a child in the amusement park”, a typically positive concept, together with a valence and arousal of (−2, −2), EmotiCrafter renders the scene as sad.

It even works without words. From an empty prompt and a valence-arousal pair alone, it generates images that hold a consistent emotion. Named emotions such as amusement, awe or sadness can be requested as points on the plane, and the control is fine-grained: in one example, a surfer’s arousal climbs from 1.8 to 2.6 in increments of 0.2 while valence stays at 1.6.

chapters.title: Other methods froze, or jumped
paragraphs: To test the idea, we built four alternatives on SDXL. Two fed emotion features into its UNet, through cross-attention based on IP-Adapter or through the time embedding; one embedded them in prompt templates with Textual Inversion; and one had GPT-4 rewrite the prompt to match the valence and arousal values.

The first three barely responded. Whatever emotion they were given, they produced nearly identical images, and Textual Inversion added a persistent purple tint. Their training aligned low-level image features that follow the prompt’s content closely but struggle to capture subtle emotional cues. GPT-4+SDXL did change the mood, but not smoothly: on a 5 × 5 grid of skiers it shows noticeable discontinuities, most visibly in the V = 3 column.

On LPIPS-Continuous, a perceptual measure of how continuously images change as the values change, EmotiCrafter scored 0.220 against 0.361 for GPT-4+SDXL, where lower is smoother. Across 3,300 images per method, it also had the lowest arousal and valence errors of the five: 1.828 and 1.510.

figures.caption: Two prompts at valence and arousal values of −1.5, 0 and 1.5. Cross Attention, Time Embedding and Textual Inversion barely change; only EmotiCrafter and GPT-4+SDXL show clear emotional variation.

“A group of people is skiing in a snow hill” across a 5 × 5 grid from −3 to 3. EmotiCrafter (top) stays continuous at the extremes; GPT-4+SDXL (bottom) shows discontinuities, for example in the V = 3 column.

chapters.title: Sorting images by feel
paragraphs: Metrics are not perception, so we asked 20 college students. In the first study, they took shuffled sets of five images, put them in order of valence or of arousal, and estimated each image’s values. Kendall’s τb measured how well their order matched the intended one, with 1 meaning perfect alignment.

The gap was widest for arousal: 0.759 with EmotiCrafter’s images against 0.165 with GPT-4+SDXL’s. Valence ordering reached 0.887, against 0.584, and participants’ estimates landed closer to the target, with errors of 1.327 versus 2.029 for arousal and 0.692 versus 1.229 for valence.

In a second study, participants rated 25-image sets that moved gradually from −3 to +3. EmotiCrafter averaged 4.215 out of 5 for following the emotional changes and 4.240 for smoothness, against 3.525 and 3.195. Every one of these differences was statistically significant.

figures.caption: User studies comparing EmotiCrafter (Ours) with GPT-4+SDXL (Baseline): ranking agreement, estimation error, and ratings of emotion consistency and smoothness (***p < 0.001).

chapters.title: What a stronger feeling costs
paragraphs: Emotion is not free. EmotiCrafter’s CLIPScore, which measures how closely an image matches its prompt, was 23.067, below the 26.566 of Time Embedding, a baseline that barely expressed emotion. The training target makes this tension explicit: the shift from neutral to emotional features is deliberately enlarged by a factor α, and as α rises, emotion errors fall while CLIPScore falls with them.

A second training choice protects rare feelings. Training images are unevenly spread across the valence-arousal plane, so each example’s loss is weighted inversely to how crowded its region is. Without this weighting, valence error rose from 1.510 to 1.546 and CLIPScore dropped from 23.067 to 21.977.

quote.text: Based on these findings, we set α = 1.5 as an optimal trade-off, though users can adjust α to suit their specific needs.

figures.caption: “An oil painting shows an astronaut” at α from 1.0 to 2.0, with and without density weighting. Higher α brings stronger emotional variation and weaker resemblance to the prompt; α = 1.5 is the chosen setting.

takeaways: Placing emotion on a continuous valence-arousal plane lets image generation express degrees of feeling, not only named categories.
Adding emotion by shifting prompt features lets what an image shows and how it feels be controlled separately.
Stronger emotion costs some fidelity to the literal prompt, a trade-off EmotiCrafter measures and leaves adjustable rather than hidden.

facts.label: Inputs
facts.value: Free-text prompt + valence and arousal values, each in [−3, 3]

facts.label: Backbone
facts.value: Stable Diffusion XL, conditioned by a GPT-2-based emotion-embedding network

facts.label: Training data
facts.value: Neutral/emotional prompt pairs built from 39,843 V-A-annotated images (OASIS, EMOTIC, FindingEmo)

facts.label: Evaluation
facts.value: 4 baselines, 3,300 images per method, 2 user studies with 20 participants

facts.label: Limitations
facts.value: Arousal is harder to control than valence; scenes often gain human activity the prompt never mentioned; prompts occasionally shift in meaning
